Emaciated

/ih-MAY-shee-ay-tid/ - the stress falls on MAY · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Emaciated means extremely thin and wasted away, especially from lack of food.

Two winters in the prison camp had left the poet so emaciated that his own brother walked past him on the station platform.

Worked Example

The workhouse inspector's 1842 report lingered on the children of the east ward: emaciated, their wrists no thicker than broom handles, they had been fed thin gruel for a year while the ledgers recorded meat.

Emaciated goes far beyond 'thin' or 'slender' — it names a body that has visibly wasted away, usually from starvation or illness. A runner is lean by training; an emaciated child has been hollowed out by hunger.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

gaunt: hollow-cheeked and bony from strain, illness, or hunger — grim, but short of emaciated's outright wasting

skeletal: so thin the bones stand out; matches emaciated's extreme without naming starvation as the cause

haggard: worn and exhausted in the face — you can be haggard after one sleepless week without losing a pound

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

plump: comfortably rounded with healthy flesh — everything an emaciated frame has lost

portly: stout and heavy through the middle; the opposite extreme of the scale

Where it sits · how starved the body looks — thin → gaunt → emaciated

thin vs. emaciated: Thin is neutral and often healthy — a thin distance runner is simply lean; thin stops far short of emaciated, which names dangerous wasting.

gaunt vs. emaciated: Gaunt is darker than thin — cheeks hollow, bones near the surface — but it still stops short of emaciated, the point where the body has plainly begun to waste away.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-

Prefix — e-: out, thoroughly - a form of ex-

Root — maci

Root — maci: leanness - Latin macies

Suffix — -ated

Suffix — -ated: made; brought to a state

Put it together

Put it together: E- (out, thoroughly) + maci- (leanness) + -ated = wasted into leanness through and through. Watch the disguise: emaciated looks like an em- 'cause to be' word, but the m belongs to the Latin root macies, 'leanness' — the prefix is e-, the 'out' prefix of exit and emit. Latin emaciare meant to waste the flesh away, and the English word keeps that clinical edge.

Use the root in a new word: meager

Use the root in a new word: meager: You met meager back in Course 1 — it grew from the same lean Latin root: the survivors lived on meager rations of rice and salt.

Root Check

Word Choice

clinical / vivid

Reach for emaciated only when a body has truly wasted — famine, illness, neglect; it belongs in doctors' notes and war reporting, and it turns insulting if aimed at someone merely slim. For ordinary thinness, say thin, lean, or slender. Its unit-mate enervated empties the batteries for an afternoon; emaciated empties the flesh itself.
